title: SAP weighs cutting at least 10,000 jobs in AI restructuring, Bloomberg says
excerpt: SAP job cuts would hit at least 9% of staff, with product, engineering and sales in focus. Its 2024 overhaul removed about 10,000 roles.
content_html:
SAP is preparing to cut at least 10,000 jobs as it reshapes its software business around AI, Christina Kyriasoglou reported for Bloomberg on Thursday, citing people familiar with the matter. That would be at least 9% of the German company’s workforce. SAP employs more than 110,000 people worldwide.

The final number has not been set and could change after talks with labour representatives, the people told Bloomberg. SAP has asked every department to find areas to cut. Product and engineering, and sales, are the main focus.

The plan would add SAP to the large software companies shrinking their workforces as they rebuild around AI. Oracle has cut 21,000 jobs in 12 months, and Microsoft is offering buyouts to 60,000 employees, Bloomberg reported.

SAP did not say whether it plans any cuts.

“SAP continuously reviews its organization to ensure it remains aligned with its strategy and customer needs,” the company said in a statement to Bloomberg.

An AI-first board

SAP has reorganised its executive board twice this year as chief executive Christian Klein pushes an AI-first strategy. In June, SAP handed AI product oversight to Klein and its chief operating officer. Klein then took over most of the duties of product chief Muhammad Alam. Alam did not renew his contract, which ends in March.

Sales chief Thomas Saueressig said last week that he will leave to run Ionos, the German cloud provider. Two of SAP’s six board members will be gone by March.

Klein wants to build AI tools into SAP’s applications. Earlier AI products ran into problems with customers, according to Bloomberg.

The last restructuring

SAP usually announces restructurings with its full-year results in late January. The last one, in 2024, removed about 10,000 positions, cost about €3bn and took more than a year. Most of it came through voluntary departures and retraining, and total headcount stayed roughly flat as SAP hired for new roles.

This year SAP froze hiring and travel in July. In Germany, where most of its staff work, the works council negotiated a job guarantee through 2028.

“Our headcount has increased a little bit over the course of the year,” chief financial officer Dominik Asam said at a Morgan Stanley conference last week.

Asam added that he “would be really surprised” if that trend did not reverse. SAP is also dealing with a partner’s complaint that one of its staff passed a startup’s demo to a rival.
